items.followUp: Define a suspension and give one example.

rubric.why: A solution is defined by its uniform composition and components.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition containing both ideas; accept equivalent wording such as uniform mixture of substances.

rubric.why: An appropriate example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as salt water or sugar solution.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
Salt water is an example of a solution.

items.followUp: Write the reaction of bromine with methane in bright sunlight.

rubric.why: The reaction equation must show the reactants and products of the substitution reaction.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, allowing equivalent notation.

rubric.why: Bright sunlight is the stated condition for the reaction.
rubric.description: Indicates the reaction occurs in bright sunlight.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting sunlight or an equivalent light condition.

modelAnswer: In bright sunlight, methane reacts with chlorine by substitution:
CH₄ + Cl₂ ⟶ CH₃Cl + HCl

items.followUp: Why does atomic size generally increase down a group?

rubric.why: The trend in size is part of the explanation for increasing electropositive character.
rubric.description: States that atomic size increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct size trend.

rubric.why: The outer electron becomes easier to remove, so the atom more readily forms a positive ion.
rubric.description: Explains that increased distance/shielding makes electron removal easier, or that ionization energy decreases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation linking the trend to easier loss of the valence electron.

modelAnswer: Down a group, atomic size and shielding effect increase.
The valence electron is farther from the nucleus and is less strongly attracted to it.
It is therefore lost more easily, so electropositive character increases.

items.followUp: State two differences between the Bohr model and the modern atomic model.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy specific allowed orbits with definite energies.
rubric.description: States that electrons move in fixed, allowed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the permitted stationary orbits or shells.

rubric.why: The absence of radiation in an allowed orbit distinguishes it from a changing orbit.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while in an allowed stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the no-radiation postulate.

rubric.why: Quantized angular momentum specifies which electron orbits are allowed.
rubric.description: Gives the angular-momentum quantization condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mvr = nh/2π or an equivalent statement.

rubric.why: Electron transitions between energy levels account for absorption or emission of energy.
rubric.description: Explains that a transition involves absorption or emission of a photon equal to the energy difference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transition rule or ΔE = hν.

rubric.why: The permitted energy states are discrete, not continuous.
rubric.description: States that electrons change between discrete energy levels, not intermediate energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explicitly identifying discrete energy levels or transitions between them.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted circular orbits called stationary orbits or energy levels.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy, and an electron does not radiate energy while it remains in that orbit.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3, …
An electron absorbs or emits energy only when it jumps between energy levels; the energy change is ΔE = hν.
The energy levels are discrete, so electrons cannot have energies between the permitted levels.

items.followUp: Define a mixture and name its two main types.

rubric.why: The definition should identify chemical combination and a fixed composition.
rubric.description: Defines a compound as two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition that includes chemical combination and fixed ratio/proportion.

rubric.why: Organic compounds are one common classification by composition.
rubric.description: Identifies organic compounds and describes them as carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming and accurately describing the organic class.

rubric.why: Inorganic compounds form the other class in this classification.
rubric.description: Identifies inorganic compounds and distinguishes them from organic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the inorganic class and giving an appropriate distinction or example.

rubric.why: Compounds can also be classified by bonding; these examples demonstrate that distinction.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example or bonding-based classification of compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming ionic and molecular/covalent compounds, or giving a correct example of either type.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements chemically combine in a fixed proportion.
By composition, compounds are classified as organic and inorganic; organic compounds are carbon compounds, while inorganic compounds include substances such as sodium chloride and water.
By the type of bonding, compounds may also be classified as ionic, such as NaCl, or molecular (covalent), such as H₂O.

items.followUp: Illustrate a polar covalent bond in HCl and a non-polar covalent bond in Cl₂.

rubric.why: A polar covalent bond involves unequal sharing and partial charges.
rubric.description: Explains and illustrates a polar covalent bond, such as Hδ+—Clδ−.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for unequal sharing and 1 mark for a correct polar example or partial charges.

rubric.why: A non-polar covalent bond involves equal sharing between atoms of the same element.
rubric.description: Explains and illustrates a non-polar covalent bond, such as Cl—Cl.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for equal sharing and 1 mark for a correct example or illustration.

rubric.why: Both examples should show that the bond is formed by sharing electrons.
rubric.description: Identifies the shared electron pair as the basis of covalent bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that covalent bonds form through shared electrons.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond forms when atoms share a pair of electrons.
In HCl, chlorine attracts the shared pair more strongly, so sharing is unequal and the bond is polar: Hδ+—Clδ−.
In Cl₂, identical chlorine atoms share the pair equally, so the bond is non-polar: Cl—Cl.

items.followUp: What is an ion? Distinguish between a cation and an anion.

rubric.why: An ion is identified by its net charge, produced by electron transfer.
rubric.description: Defines an ion as an atom or group of atoms with a net electric charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including charge or gain/loss of electrons.

rubric.why: The two types are distinguished by the signs of their charges.
rubric.description: Names the positive ion (cation) and negative ion (anion).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both types with the correct charge signs.

modelAnswer: An ion is an atom or group of atoms carrying a net electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons.
Its types are cations, which are positively charged, and anions, which are negatively charged.

items.followUp: Calculate the number of moles in 36 g of water.

rubric.why: Correct SI data are needed for the calculation.
rubric.description: States the mass and molar mass of water in SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 9 g = 0.009 kg and the molar mass of water = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹.

rubric.why: The mole formula and substitution establish the calculation.
rubric.description: Uses the formula n = m/M and substitutes the values with units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct formula and substitution.

rubric.why: The calculation gives half a mole of water.
rubric.description: Gives the correct number of moles with a unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 0.5 mol.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 9 g = 0.009 kg; molar mass of H₂O, M = 18 g mol⁻¹ = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = m/M.
Substitution: n = 0.009 kg ÷ 0.018 kg mol⁻¹.
Answer: n = 0.5 mol.
